title: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc.

content.overview: Section 69 BNS codifies a brand-new substantive offence penalizing sexual intercourse by deceitful means or through a false promise of marriage made without any intention of fulfillment, where the act does not amount to rape. Punishable with imprisonment up to ten years and fine, this provision statutorily resolves decades of conflicting jurisprudence under the erstwhile Section 375/90 IPC regime. The statutory Explanation defines deceitful means to include inducement for employment or promotion, as well as marriage by suppressing true identity. Article 20(1) mandates strictly prospective application to acts committed on or after 1 July 2024.

content.study:
I. LEGISLATIVE GENESIS & THE POST-IPC PARADIGM SHIFT
Section 69 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) represents one of the most significant substantive innovations in Indian criminal jurisprudence, situated in Chapter V ("Of Offences Against Woman and Child"). Under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the statute contained no specific provision addressing sexual relations induced by fraudulent promises or deceptive inducements. Consequently, prosecutors were compelled to force these cases into the straitjacket of Rape under Section 375/376 IPC by invoking Section 90 IPC ("consent given under a misconception of fact").

This legal fiction led to profound jurisprudential uncertainty. In a long line of decisions—including Uday v. State of Karnataka (2003) 4 SCC 46, Deelip Singh v. State of Bihar (2005) 1 SCC 88, Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra (2019) 9 SCC 608, Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh (2019) 10 SCC 326, and Sonu @ Subhash Kumar v. State of U.P. (2021) 18 SCC 517—the Supreme Court repeatedly struggled to distinguish between a false promise to marry made deceitfully ab initio and a genuine breach of promise caused by subsequent familial, caste, or socio-economic discord.

To eradicate this artificial conflation of violent non-consensual rape with consensual intimacy induced by deception, Parliament enacted Section 69 BNS as an independent, self-contained penal offence carrying a maximum sentence of ten years, preserving Section 63/64 BNS exclusively for non-consensual sexual violations.

II. STATUTORY TEXT & ESSENTIAL INGREDIENTS
Section 69 provides:
"Whoever, by deceitful means or by making promise to marry to a woman without any intention of fulfilling the same, has sexual intercourse with her, such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine.
Explanation.—“deceitful means” shall include inducement for, or false promise of employment or promotion, or marrying by suppressing identity."

Essential Ingredients:
1. Sexual Intercourse: The accused must have engaged in sexual intercourse with the complainant woman.
2. Causal Inducement through Deceit or False Promise: The sexual intercourse must have been induced either by:
   (a) Deceitful means (as expanded by the statutory Explanation); OR
   (b) A promise to marry made without any intention of fulfilling the same at the time of making the promise.
3. Negative Limiting Gateway: "Such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape." The encounter must be consensual in fact, where consent was procured through fraud or deception rather than physical force, duress, or under-age statutory bar under Section 63 BNS.
4. Penal Sanction: Imprisonment of either description extending up to ten years, and mandatory fine.

III. DECONSTRUCTING "DECEITFUL MEANS" & THE STATUTORY EXPLANATION
The Explanation to Section 69 provides an inclusive, non-exhaustive definition of "deceitful means" comprising three distinct statutory categories:
1. False Promise or Inducement of Employment: Where a person in a corporate, institutional, or administrative position induces a woman to engage in sexual intimacy under the fraudulent assurance of securing employment.
2. False Promise or Inducement of Promotion: Quid pro quo sexual exploitation in workplace hierarchies where career advancement is dishonestly promised.
3. Marrying by Suppressing Identity: Engaging in marriage or cohabitation by concealing true personal identity, including existing subsisting marriage, religious identity, caste, or civil status.

IV. THE DOCTRINE OF INTENTION AB INITIO VS SUBSEQUENT BREACH
The core jurisprudential battleground under Section 69 is the accused's state of mind at the inception of the promise:
1. Pramod Suryabhan Pawar Doctrine Codified:
   - To establish the offence under the second limb of Section 69, the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the promise to marry was false from the very inception—that the accused had no intention whatsoever of fulfilling it when it was made, and used it purely as a tool of seduction.
   - If the accused genuinely intended to marry the complainant at the time the relationship commenced, but the marriage could not materialize due to subsequent unforeseen events, family opposition, horoscope mismatches, or irreconcilable emotional differences, the act constitutes a bona fide breach of promise and does NOT attract Section 69 BNS.
2. Evidentiary Burden under BSA Section 104:
   - The burden rests squarely upon the prosecution to demonstrate fraudulent intention ab initio. The mere subsequent refusal to marry does not generate a retrospective presumption of criminal deceit.

V. CONSTITUTIONAL PROSPECTIVITY & SECTION 531 BNSS PROCEDURAL INTERFACE
1. Absolute Bar against Retrospective Penalization (Article 20(1)):
   - Section 69 creates a new substantive offence carrying a severe penalty of up to ten years. Under Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India, no person can be prosecuted or convicted under Section 69 BNS for acts of sexual intercourse or promises made prior to 1 July 2024.
   - Any FIR registered under Section 69 BNS for pre-July 2024 relationships is unconstitutional and liable to be quashed under Section 528 BNSS (old s. 482 CrPC).
2. Procedural Epochs under Section 531(2)(a) BNSS:
   - For acts occurring prior to 1 July 2024, the prosecution must proceed under IPC Section 376/417 read with Section 90 IPC, subject to the stringent filters of Pramod Suryabhan Pawar.
   - For acts occurring on or after 1 July 2024, Section 69 BNS is the exclusive, proper charge.

VI. DIGITAL EVIDENCE & SECTION 63 BSA ADMISSIBILITY
In modern Section 69 prosecutions, proving or disproving intent ab initio relies predominantly on contemporaneous electronic communications:
- WhatsApp chats, SMS threads, emails, and call recordings are critical to demonstrating whether the parties engaged in mutual long-term emotional intimacy, attempted to persuade families, or whether the accused deployed false identities, fictitious profiles, or fraudulent employment appointment letters.
- All digital records tendered by prosecution or defence must strictly comply with the certification mandate of Section 63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

sections.heading: The legal rule
sections.body:
69. Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc.—Whoever, by deceitful means or by making promise to marry to a woman without any intention of fulfilling the same, has sexual intercourse with her, such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine.
Explanation.—“deceitful means” shall include inducement for, or false promise of employment or promotion, or marrying by suppressing identity.

sections.heading: Legislative Architecture & Historical Resolution of Section 375/90 IPC Quagmire
sections.body:
Section 69 BNS creates a new substantive penal offence in Chapter V, prescribing imprisonment up to ten years and fine.
Eliminates the historical conflation under the colonial IPC where sexual relations under broken promises were prosecuted as violent rape under Section 376 read with Section 90 IPC.
Codifies a balanced legislative solution protecting women against deceitful exploitation while shielding consensual relationships from vexatious rape charges.
The negative gateway clause ("such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape") delineates Section 69 from Section 63 BNS.

sections.heading: The Two Substantive Limbs: Deceitful Means vs False Promise of Marriage
sections.body:
Limb 1: Sexual intercourse procured by deceitful means, specifically including false promises of employment, promotion, or marriage by concealing identity.
Limb 2: Sexual intercourse procured by making a promise to marry without any intention of fulfilling the same from the inception.
The offence requires positive proof of causal nexus: the deceit or false promise must be the direct inducing cause of the sexual intercourse.
Where intimacy was based on mutual passion or long-standing affection rather than induced by the promise, Section 69 is not attracted.

sections.heading: Doctrinal Threshold: False Promise ab initio vs Bona Fide Breach of Promise
sections.body:
The Supreme Court in Pramod Suryabhan Pawar (2019) and Sonu @ Subhash Kumar (2021) established that breach of promise is fundamentally civil, not criminal, unless fraudulent ab initio.
Prosecution must present concrete evidence that the accused harboured a deceitful mens rea at the exact time the promise was uttered.
Subsequent breakdown of marriage negotiations due to caste objections, dowry disputes, parental resistance, or incompatibility does not constitute Section 69.
Conduct of the accused immediately before and after the promise (e.g. introducing partner to parents, booking wedding halls) negates criminal deceit.

sections.heading: Deceitful Means: Employment Inducement, Promotion & Identity Suppression
sections.body:
Statutory Explanation explicitly codifies workplace quid pro quo sexual exploitation through fraudulent offers of job appointments or promotions.
Suppressing identity covers concealment of existing subsisting marriage, true name, age, religious faith, or civil status.
Where an already-married man falsely represents himself as a bachelor to induce a woman into marriage or physical intimacy, the case falls squarely within Section 69 Explanation.
Such acts also interface with Section 82 BNS (cohabitation caused by a man deceitfully inducing a belief of lawful marriage).

sections.heading: Constitutional Prospectivity (Art. 20(1)), BSA s. 63 Proof & Trial Practice
sections.body:
Article 20(1) of the Constitution mandates that Section 69 BNS applies strictly to acts committed on or after 1 July 2024; retroactive application is unconstitutional.
Section 531(2)(a) BNSS preserves IPC Section 376/417 for conduct occurring prior to the commencement date.
Evidentiary substantiation relies heavily on electronic records; WhatsApp chats, audio notes, and travel reservations must be certified under Section 63(4) BSA.
Remedies against malicious FIRs: Application for quashing under Section 528 BNSS before the High Court where chats demonstrate a consensual relationship and bona fide subsequent fallout.

examples.title: False Promise of Employment by Corporate Superior — Section 69 Explanation
examples.body: Managing Director M interviews applicant A for an executive position. M falsely informs A that she has been shortlisted, creates a fake internal appointment memorandum, and takes A to a hotel claiming it is an official orientation weekend. In the hotel, M promises A that she will be confirmed in the role if she shares a bed with him. Relying entirely on this assurance, A engages in sexual intercourse. Two days later, M terminates communication and appoints his relative. Forensic records and WhatsApp messages establish that M never submitted A’s name to HR and fabricated the memorandum. M is charged and convicted under Section 69 BNS for procuring sexual intercourse by deceitful means (false promise of employment) and sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment.

examples.title: Bona Fide Consensual Relationship and Eventual Family Discord — Section 69 Excluded
examples.body: Boyfriend B and Girlfriend G, both aged 25, enter into an affectionate consensual relationship spanning three years, during which they cohabit and engage in physical relations. B introduces G to his parents and opens a joint bank account for marriage expenses. Subsequently, severe inter-caste opposition from B’s extended family leads to intense pressure, causing B to call off the engagement. G registers an FIR under Section 69 BNS alleging sexual intercourse under false promise of marriage. In quashing proceedings under Section 528 BNSS, the High Court finds that B genuinely intended to marry G from inception and that the subsequent breakdown was a bona fide failure of engagement, not deceit ab initio. The FIR under Section 69 BNS is quashed.

hypotheticals.question: As Senior Counsel advising the prosecution, frame the legal submissions demonstrating that R’s conduct satisfies all ingredients of Section 69 BNS read with its Explanation.
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Inapplicability of Pure Consensual Defence:
   - R cannot claim consensual immunity because S’s agreement to sexual intercourse was directly induced by R’s fraudulent representation of being an unmarried bachelor eligible to marry her.
2. Satisfaction of "Deceitful Means" under Section 69 Explanation:
   - The statutory Explanation explicitly provides that "deceitful means" shall include "marrying by suppressing identity". R systematically suppressed his true name, religious identity, and subsisting marriage.
   - R’s promise to marry was legally impossible and false ab initio because, as an already-married man under secular/civil laws or without disclosing his marital status, he had no legal capacity or intention to contract a valid marriage with S.
3. Alignment with Anurag Soni (2019):
   - In Anurag Soni, the Supreme Court held that where an accused was already engaged or married to someone else while making a promise of marriage to another woman, his intention was dishonest from the very beginning.
4. Non-Amointing to Rape Clause:
   - Because the act occurred through psychological deceit rather than physical coercion or force, it does not amount to violent rape under Section 63 BNS, making Section 69 the exact statutory home for prosecution.

misconceptions.trap: Believing that every relationship where marriage does not materialize results in an offence under Section 69 BNS.
misconceptions.correction: The Supreme Court in Pramod Suryabhan Pawar (2019) and Sonu @ Subhash Kumar (2021) firmly established that a bona fide breach of promise due to family opposition or subsequent incompatibility is not criminal. Prosecution must prove deceitful intention ab initio.

misconceptions.trap: Applying Section 69 BNS retrospectively to sexual encounters that took place before 1 July 2024.
misconceptions.correction: Under Article 20(1) of the Constitution, ex post facto criminal laws are unconstitutional. Section 69 creates a brand-new offence and applies solely to acts committed on or after 1 July 2024. Pre-commencement conduct must be evaluated under IPC Sections 376/417 read with Section 90 IPC.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming Section 69 BNS is an aggravated form of Rape under Section 63/64 BNS.
misconceptions.correction: Section 69 is an independent, distinct offence that explicitly requires that the sexual intercourse must "not amount to the offence of rape". It sits outside the mandatory minimum sentencing regime of Section 64.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Senior Counsel Legal Assessment: Scope and Ingredients of Section 69 BNS
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. STATUTORY ARCHITECTURE & GENESIS
Section 69 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) is a pioneering substantive provision in Chapter V ("Of Offences Against Woman and Child"). It codifies the distinct offence of sexual intercourse by deceitful means or through a false promise of marriage, resolving the historical flaw of prosecuting such cases as rape under Section 375/90 IPC.

II. ESSENTIAL INGREDIENTS
To secure a conviction under Section 69 BNS, the prosecution must establish:
1. That the accused had sexual intercourse with the complainant woman;
2. That such intercourse was procured either:
   (a) By deceitful means (including false promise of employment, promotion, or marriage by suppressing identity); OR
   (b) By making a promise to marry without any intention of fulfilling the same at the inception;
3. That such sexual intercourse does not amount to the offence of rape under Section 63 BNS;
4. That the accused acted with dishonest and fraudulent mens rea at the time the inducement was offered.

III. STATUTORY EXPLANATION & SCOPE
The Explanation expands "deceitful means" to encompass:
- Inducement for or false promise of employment;
- False promise of promotion;
- Marrying by suppressing identity (e.g. concealing existing subsisting marriage or true identity).

IV. PUNISHMENT & CLASSIFICATION
Imprisonment of either description extending up to ten years, and fine. The offence is cognizable, non-bailable, and triable by the Court of Session.

V. CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITATION
Under Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India and Section 531(2)(a) BNSS, Section 69 BNS operates strictly prospectively for acts committed on or after 1 July 2024.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Appellate / Section 528 BNSS Quashing Submissions: Distinguishing Breach of Promise from Section 69 BNS
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
MAY IT PLEASE YOUR LORDSHIPS:

1. JURISDICTION & PRAYER:
This petition under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) seeks quashing of FIR No. 142/2024 registered under Section 69 BNS. It is submitted that the uncontroverted allegations do not disclose the commission of any cognizable offence.

2. ABSENCE OF DECEITFUL INTENTION AB INITIO (PRAMOD SURYABHAN PAWAR DOCTRINE):
(a) To attract the penal sanctions of Section 69 BNS, the prosecution must demonstrate that the petitioner harboured a dishonest intention from the very inception of the promise to marry.
(b) In Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra (2019) 9 SCC 608 and Sonu @ Subhash Kumar v. State of U.P. (2021) 18 SCC 517, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that there is a fundamental distinction between a false promise to marry made deceitfully to induce sexual relations, and a breach of promise caused by subsequent unforeseen circumstances.
(c) The record discloses that the petitioner and the respondent were in a consensual relationship for over two years. The petitioner introduced the respondent to his parents and booked a banquet hall for the engagement ceremony (Annexure P-4). The eventual cancellation occurred due to serious financial and dowry disputes between the elders, entirely beyond the petitioner’s control.

3. ADMISSION OF CONTEMPORANEOUS ELECTRONIC RECORDS (BSA SECTION 63):
The WhatsApp conversations between the parties, certified under Section 63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Annexure P-6), reveal that the sexual intimacy was a product of mutual emotional attachment and passion, rather than induced by a fraudulent promise. A subsequent breakdown of a consensual adult relationship cannot be retrospectively converted into a criminal offence under Section 69 BNS.

4. ABUSE OF CRIMINAL PROCESS & PRAYER FOR QUASHING:
The continuation of criminal proceedings against the petitioner amounts to a manifest abuse of the process of the court. In terms of State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335, where the allegations in the FIR do not prima facie constitute an offence, the High Court is duty-bound to exercise its inherent jurisdiction under Section 528 BNSS.

It is therefore respectfully prayed that FIR No. 142/2024 and all consequential proceedings arising therefrom be quashed in the interest of justice.

cases.name: Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra
cases.holding: The Supreme Court laid down the definitive test for consent under promise of marriage: to constitute an offence, the promise must be false from the very inception and must have a direct causal nexus with the decision to engage in sexual intercourse. A subsequent breach due to unforeseen reasons does not amount to criminal fraud.

cases.name: Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh
cases.holding: Held that where an accused made a promise of marriage to the prosecutrix while already having arranged his marriage with another woman, his promise was demonstrably false ab initio and designed purely to induce sexual relations, establishing criminal deceit.

cases.name: Sonu @ Subhash Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.holding: Reiterated that consensual sexual intercourse between two adults during an ongoing courtship cannot be treated as rape or criminal deceit simply because the marriage could not materialize due to family opposition.

cases.name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
cases.holding: Established the landmark guidelines for exercising inherent powers (now under Section 528 BNSS) to quash criminal proceedings where the uncontroverted allegations do not disclose any cognizable offence or where the prosecution is manifestly malicious.

examTips: Always emphasize that Section 69 BNS is a brand-new substantive offence with no direct predecessor in the IPC.
Remember the negative limiting clause: Section 69 applies only where sexual intercourse "does not amount to the offence of rape". If physical force or violence is present, charge Section 63/64 BNS.
Under Article 20(1) of the Constitution, Section 69 cannot be applied retrospectively; acts occurring prior to 1 July 2024 must be evaluated under IPC Sections 376/417 read with Section 90 IPC.
Identify the two distinct branches: (1) deceitful means (employment/promotion/identity suppression), and (2) promise to marry without intention to fulfill ab initio.
Highlight that a bona fide breach of promise due to subsequent circumstances does not attract Section 69 BNS (Pramod Suryabhan Pawar).

examFrameworks.question: Structured Chamber Brief: Analyzing Liability under Section 69 BNS
steps: Confirm prospective applicability under Article 20(1) of the Constitution (act on or after 1 July 2024).
Verify that the sexual intercourse was consensual in fact, satisfying the gateway condition ("not amounting to rape").
Analyze whether the inducement falls under "deceitful means" (employment, promotion, identity suppression) or "promise to marry".
Evaluate evidence of intention ab initio under Pramod Suryabhan Pawar vs subsequent bona fide breach.
Review electronic evidence compliance under Section 63 BSA (WhatsApp, call records, emails).
Conclude on maintainability of charge or grounds for quashing under Section 528 BNSS.

examFrameworks.question: Defense Strategy: Petition for Quashing FIR under Section 528 BNSS for Section 69 BNS Charge
steps: Invoke Bhajan Lal categories 1 and 7 (allegations do not disclose offence and proceeding is malicious).
Demonstrate multi-year consensual relationship and mutual emotional attachment.
Produce certified digital communications under Section 63 BSA showing active steps towards marriage.
Establish the exact external event (e.g. family discord, horoscope, dowry dispute) causing breakdown of engagement.
Show absence of deceit ab initio and pray for quashing of FIR.

enhancement.definition: BNS s. 69 penalizes sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means or promise to marry without any intention of fulfilling it. It provides: Whoever, by deceitful means or by making a promise to marry to a woman without any intention of fulfilling the same, and has sexual intercourse with her, such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. enhancement.legalPrinciple: Protection of female bodily autonomy against fraud, deception, and identity concealment. Consent obtained through active deception, bad faith promises, or suppressed identity is invalid, constituting a specific non-rape felony carrying up to ten years imprisonment.
statutoryFramework: Chapter V — Of Offences against Women and Children, BNS s. 69.
Core Actus Reus: Having sexual intercourse with a woman, not amounting to the offence of rape under Section 63.
Culpable Means: Employing deceitful means, or making a promise to marry without any intention of fulfilling the same.
The Explanation: Deceitful means defined to include false promise of employment or promotion, inducement, or marrying after suppressing identity.
Sentencing Framework: Imprisonment of either description extending up to ten years, plus mandatory fine; cognizable and non-bailable.
essentialIngredients: The accused had sexual intercourse with the victim woman.
The sexual intercourse does not amount to rape under Section 63 (it is based on apparent consent procured through deception).
The consent of the woman was obtained by either:
(a) Making a promise to marry her without any intention of fulfilling the promise from the inception; or
(b) Employing deceitful means, including false promises of employment, promotion, fraudulent inducement, or marrying after suppressing real identity.
The existence of fraudulent intent (bad faith) at the very moment the promise or representation was made.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 69 BNS represents one of the most significant and widely debated substantive additions in India’s criminal law reform. Under the repealed Indian Penal Code, 1860, there was no specific offence covering sexual relations obtained through a false promise of marriage or deceptive identity; prosecutors were compelled to charge the accused with rape under Section 375/376 IPC relying on Section 90 IPC (consent given under a misconception of fact).

This historical practice created immense judicial difficulty. Courts struggled to distinguish between (a) a genuine consensual relationship where marriage later failed due to family opposition, cultural differences, or circumstances (which is not a crime), and (b) a predatory deception where the accused never intended to marry the woman and used the promise solely to induce sexual intercourse.

Section 69 resolves this dilemma by creating an autonomous, specific offence distinct from rape. It requires proof that the accused had **no intention of fulfilling the promise from the very inception**. Furthermore, the Explanation explicitly encompasses cases of **identity suppression** (such as concealing religious identity, marital status, or criminal background to obtain sexual relations) and false inducements of government employment or commercial promotions. The maximum sentence of ten years reflects the grave moral culpability while distinguishing it from the minimum ten-year-to-life sentences applicable to rape.
examples: Teaching illustration (Suppression of Identity): Accused A creates a fake social media profile under a false name, suppressing his real marital status and religion. He promises marriage to victim B and has sexual intercourse with her. Upon discovering his true identity, B lodges a complaint. A is liable under Section 69 BNS for sexual intercourse by deceitful means (marrying after suppressing identity).

Teaching illustration (Bona Fide Breach of Promise vs Crime): C and D are in a mutual romantic relationship for two years with an honest intention to marry. Later, due to unexpected severe family opposition and financial ruin, C is unable to marry D. C is not liable under Section 69 BNS: the breach of promise was not fraudulent from the inception, and consent was not procured through deceitful means.
distinctions: BNS s. 69 vs BNS s. 63 (Rape): Section 63 penalizes non-consensual sexual acts (or consent under fear/unsoundness); Section 69 explicitly applies to intercourse "not amounting to the offence of rape" where apparent consent is procured through false promise of marriage or deceitful means.

BNS s. 69 vs Civil Breach of Contract: A mere breach of promise to marry without proof of dishonest intention from the very beginning gives rise only to civil remedies; criminal liability under Section 69 requires mens rea of bad faith from the inception.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who promised a woman a job in a government ministry and had sexual relations with her on that premise, knowing he had no power or intention to provide the job, is guilty under Section 69 BNS.

Rule: Under the Explanation to Section 69 BNS, "deceitful means" expressly includes a false promise of employment or promotion; inducing sexual intercourse through such false promise constitutes an offence punishable with up to ten years imprisonment.
Application: The accused intentionally made a false representation regarding government employment to induce the woman into sexual intercourse, satisfying the statutory definition of deceitful means.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under Section 69 BNS and liable to imprisonment extending up to ten years and fine.
